chapter.title: What Are Design Patterns? Why Use Them?

payload.markdown: Patterns define objects and solutions in object-oriented terms. This means that many patterns apply equally in more than one language. When I first started using patterns, I read code examples in C++ and Smalltalk and then deployed my solutions in Java. Others transfer with modifications to the pattern’s applicability or consequences, but remain valid. Either way, patterns can help you as you move between languages. Equally, an application that is built on good object-oriented design principles can be relatively easy to port between languages (although there are always issues that must be addressed).

items: Design Principles: Guidelines such as SOLID that keep object designs flexible.
Behavioral Patterns: Patterns that distribute responsibility and coordinate behaviour.
Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Creational Patterns: Patterns that control how objects come into being.
Enterprise Patterns: Patterns for service layers, domain objects and application architecture.
Error Patterns: Repeatable strategies: fail fast, wrap and rethrow, aggregate and report.
Factory Pattern: Creating objects through a dedicated creator instead of new at every call site.
Object Identity: === compares instance identity: two objects with equal fields are still distinct.
